title: Suspense and Code Splitting with React.lazy

subChunks.title: Suspense and Code Splitting with React.lazy
subChunks.hookHtml: A single large JavaScript bundle delays your app's first meaningful paint. Code splitting breaks the bundle into smaller chunks that load on demand — users only download code for features they actually visit. React's lazy and Suspense make route-level code splitting a few lines of configuration.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem: large bundles

Without code splitting, all your components ship in one bundle. A user visiting the homepage downloads the admin panel, settings page, and every other route — most of which they'll never visit.

React.lazy — dynamic import

import { lazy } from 'react';

// The import() call is only executed when the component is first rendered:
const AdminPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/AdminPage'));
const SettingsPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/SettingsPage'));

The dynamic import() returns a Promise. React waits for it to resolve before rendering the component. While waiting, React looks for the nearest <Suspense> boundary and renders its fallback.

Suspense — the loading boundary

import { Suspense, lazy } from 'react';

const AdminPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/AdminPage'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/admin" element={<AdminPage />} />
      </Routes>
    </Suspense>
  );
}

Route-level code splitting — the most impactful pattern

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';
import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

const Home     = lazy(() => import('./pages/Home'));
const Quests   = lazy(() => import('./pages/Quests'));
const Settings = lazy(() => import('./pages/Settings'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<LoadingSpinner />}>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/"        element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/quests"  element={<Quests />} />
        <Route path="/settings" element={<Settings />} />
      </Routes>
    </Suspense>
  );
}

Now each page only downloads when first navigated to. Subsequent visits use the browser cache.

Named exports and lazy

lazy() expects a module with a default export. If your component uses a named export, wrap it:

// If QuestList is a named export:
const QuestList = lazy(() =>
  import('./QuestList').then(mod => ({ default: mod.QuestList }))
);

Vex: "The split point is natural: the router. Each route is a feature boundary. Users navigate between features, not between components. Put Suspense at the router level and each page loads independently."

Error boundary + Suspense — the complete pattern

// Error boundary catches load failures; Suspense shows the loading state:
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Failed to load page.</p>}>
  <Suspense fallback={<LoadingSpinner />}>
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/admin" element={<AdminPage />} />
    </Routes>
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>

storyBeats.text: Vex opens a library with a thousand tomes. 'You do not carry all books to a visitor,' she says. 'You fetch the one they need.' She hands a single volume to a waiting scholar. 'Code splitting works the same way.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The router is the natural split point. Each route is a feature. Users navigate between features. Wrap your routes in Suspense, lazy-import each page, and your bundle breaks apart for free.

storyBeats.speaker: Route-level splitting
storyBeats.text:
const AdminPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/AdminPage'));

<Suspense fallback={<LoadingSpinner />}>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/admin" element={<AdminPage />} />
  </Routes>
</Suspense>

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Set up route-level code splitting:

  • Lazy-import two page components: HomePageLazy and AboutPageLazy
  • Wrap the <Routes> in a <Suspense> with a <p data-testid="loading">Loading...</p> fallback
  • Each page renders an <h1 data-testid="home"> or <h1 data-testid="about">
  • Wrap the Suspense in an ErrorBoundary
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a three-route app from scratch with full code-splitting: a Suspense loading state, an ErrorBoundary fallback, and three lazy-loaded pages. Add a custom LoadingSpinner component shown during transitions. Demonstrate that the ErrorBoundary catches a page that throws on render.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain code splitting to a developer who ships a 2MB bundle. What is the problem, what does React.lazy do, what does Suspense do, and where is the best place to split? Include what happens if the dynamic import fails.

options: Creates a component that dynamically imports MyPage the first time it is rendered, loading it on demand
Pre-loads MyPage immediately when the module is imported
Creates a cached version of MyPage that never re-renders
Splits MyPage into a separate file at build time without affecting runtime loading
questions.answer: Creates a component that dynamically imports MyPage the first time it is rendered, loading it on demand
questions.explanation: lazy() wraps a dynamic import(). The import is only executed when the lazy component is first rendered — not when the module containing the lazy() call is loaded. Until the import resolves, React renders the nearest Suspense fallback.

questions.prompt: A lazy-loaded component is loading. What does React render while waiting?
options: The fallback prop of the nearest ancestor <Suspense> boundary
Nothing — the page is blank until the import resolves
An automatic loading spinner from React's built-in styles
questions.answer: The fallback prop of the nearest ancestor <Suspense> boundary
questions.explanation: Suspense boundaries work like error boundaries — they catch the 'loading' signal from lazy components and render their fallback JSX. When the import resolves, React re-renders the tree with the actual component. There is no built-in spinner — you provide your own fallback.

questions.prompt: Where is the most impactful place to apply code splitting in a React app?
options: At route boundaries — each top-level page becomes its own chunk so users only download code for routes they visit
Every component should be lazy-loaded for maximum splitting
At the component library level — import only the UI components you use
Inside individual components when they have more than 100 lines of logic
questions.answer: At route boundaries — each top-level page becomes its own chunk so users only download code for routes they visit
questions.explanation: Route boundaries are natural feature boundaries. Users navigate between routes, not between individual components. Splitting at the route level is simple, high-impact, and doesn't complicate component architecture. Splitting every component creates dozens of tiny network requests and complicates the loading experience.
